title: Win a Date with Tad Hamilton!
full_review:
In 2001, director Robert Luketic -- with a little help from Reese Witherspoon's infectious smile -- charmed audiences with his feature film debut, "Legally Blonde." In his follow-up effort, "Win a Date With Tad Hamilton!" (Dreamworks), a breezy but slight teen romantic comedy, Luketic once again pins his hopes of box-office success squarely on the ditzy dimples of a bubbly towhead.

Kate Bosworth stars as Rosalee Futch, a starry-eyed grocery clerk from rural Fraziers Bottom, W.Va. When not bagging groceries at the Piggly Wiggly supermarket, where she works with her two best friends, Cathy (Ginnifer Goodwin) and Pete (Topher Grace), Rosalee can be found worshiping Hollywood heartthrob Tad Hamilton (played with appropriate self-absorption by former soap-star hottie Josh Duhamel) down at the local multiplex. Of course Pete's sarcastic quips about Hamilton have less to do with the actor's cheesy movies and Ken-doll looks than they do with Pete's own hopeless, though unspoken, infatuation for Rosalee.

When an incriminating tabloid story threatens to blow the cover off the screen stud's all-American boy-next-door image and expose him for the narcissistic rake he really is, Hamilton's agent (Nathan Lane) and manager (Sean Hayes) -- both named Richard Levy -- kick into damage-control mode and cook up the "Win a Date" contest. And guess who wins? If you guessed little ol' Rosalee Futch from Fraziers Bottom, W.Va., you've just won a date with Tad Hamilton!

So giddy she can barely string more than three words together coherently, Rosalie wings it out to the West Coast to claim her prize. But the publicity stunt yields unintended results when the hunky movie star falls for his cooing fan's effervescent charm. Having glimpsed his own shallowness in the mirror of Rosalee's unsullied naivete, Hamilton pledges to clean up his act.

In his quest for homespun wholesomeness he decides to temporarily abandon the glitz and glamour of Tinseltown and try to reconnect with his inner-bumpkin by relocating to -- guess where?

All this suits Rosalee -- and Fraziers Bottom's female population -- just fine. But Rosalee's dream come true proves to be lovesick Pete's worst nightmare, setting the stage for the ensuing competition for her affections.

Back in the 1980s director John Hughes redefined the teen genre with such youthful fluff as "Pretty in Pink" (1986) and "Some Kind of Wonderful" (1987), both of which dealt with similar triangular romances involving best friends and an out-of-their-league third party. While neither was a great movie, Hughes struck a chord with his adolescent audience by speaking their language and populating his stories with characters they could identify with. His films resonated with authenticity and celebrated the awkward quirkiness of the kids watching in the theater. By comparison, "Win a Date," with its derivative script and generically good-looking cast, feels as manufactured as, well, a Tad Hamilton film.

One aspect shared with the more innocent style of Hughes' oeuvre is the film's avoidance of the trend toward gross-out scatological and lewd humor de rigueur in many teen comedies. And though "Win a Date" contains some sexual innuendo and banter, Rosalee and Tad's romancing remains unconsummated, never evolving past heavy necking in the front seat of Tad's convertible. The only scene which affords the couple an opportunity to ratchet their passions into full gear is interrupted by a knock at the door by his handlers -- seemingly to Rosalee's relief.

However, while the film offers some good-natured insider ribbing of celebrity worship and the superficiality which fame engenders, it also tends toward a stereotypical treatment of small-town life. Many of the residents of Fraziers Bottom are portrayed as star-struck rubes who spout exclamations like "shake-a-do" and who serve more as punch lines than as characters.

In the end, this sweet but inconsequential confection is only a tad entertaining.

Due to some sexual humor and innuendo, as well as sporadic crude language and a few instances of alcohol abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
